obj-2.3-source-q009.whyItSeems: 'devices' is a natural, intuitive English word for describing connected equipment, making 'show lldp devices' feel like a reasonable guess if the exact required IOS keyword ('neighbor,' not 'devices') isn't specifically memorized.
obj-2.3-source-q009.whyWrongHere: 'show lldp devices' is not valid, recognized Cisco IOS syntax — there is no 'devices' keyword in the LLDP show command family. The correct, standard command uses the keyword 'neighbor' (or 'neighbors'): show lldp neighbor detail.
obj-2.3-source-q009.memoryAnchor: IOS LLDP commands use the specific keyword 'neighbor,' not the more intuitive-sounding but incorrect 'devices.'
obj-2.3-source-q009.contrast: show lldp neighbor detail is the real, IOS-recognized command using the correct 'neighbor' keyword; 'show lldp devices' is an invented phrase using a plausible but nonexistent keyword.

obj-2.3-source-q009.misconceptionReason: Learners substitute the Cisco-proprietary CDP command for the LLDP-specific command, confusing the two related but distinct neighbor-discovery protocols and their separate, non-interchangeable 'show' commands.
obj-2.3-source-q009.whyItSeems: Since CDP and LLDP perform the same functional role and are taught together, and 'show cdp neighbor detail' is a valid, real, frequently-practiced command, it's easy to substitute it when the question actually asks specifically about LLDP.
obj-2.3-source-q009.whyWrongHere: show cdp neighbor detail displays CDP-discovered neighbors only — it has no visibility into devices discovered via the separate LLDP protocol. To see LLDP-specific neighbor information (needed for non-Cisco device discovery, for example), the distinct command show lldp neighbor detail must be used instead.
obj-2.3-source-q009.memoryAnchor: CDP and LLDP are separate protocols with separate, non-interchangeable show commands — 'show cdp neighbor detail' never reveals LLDP-discovered neighbors, and vice versa.
obj-2.3-source-q009.contrast: show cdp neighbor detail reveals only devices discovered via Cisco's proprietary CDP; show lldp neighbor detail reveals only devices discovered via the separate, IEEE-standard LLDP protocol — running one never substitutes for the other.

obj-2.3-source-q010.misconceptionReason: Learners confuse LLDP's default advertisement interval with CDP's default interval (60 seconds), mixing up the two related but functionally distinct protocols' default timer values.
obj-2.3-source-q010.whyItSeems: Since CDP and LLDP are taught as closely related, functionally similar neighbor-discovery protocols, and CDP's actual default interval IS 60 seconds, it's easy to accidentally apply CDP's number to an LLDP question if the two protocols' distinct timers aren't kept separate in memory.
obj-2.3-source-q010.whyWrongHere: LLDP's default advertisement interval is specifically 30 seconds — twice as fast as CDP's 60-second default. 60 seconds is actually CDP's timer value, a different (though related) protocol; applying it to LLDP is a common but avoidable mix-up.
obj-2.3-source-q010.memoryAnchor: LLDP defaults to 30 seconds; CDP defaults to 60 seconds — LLDP transmits twice as often by default, don't swap the two protocols' timers.
obj-2.3-source-q010.contrast: LLDP sends an advertisement every 30 seconds by default; CDP, the Cisco-proprietary alternative, sends its advertisements half as often, every 60 seconds by default.

obj-2.3-source-q010.misconceptionReason: Learners guess a plausible-sounding but incorrect intermediate value (90 seconds) that doesn't correspond to any actual LLDP default timer, similar to the same kind of guessing error seen with CDP-related timer questions.
obj-2.3-source-q010.whyItSeems: 90 seconds is a 'round-sounding' guess that could plausibly split some difference between other timer values discussed in this topic area, making it feel like a reasonable guess if the exact 30-second LLDP figure isn't confidently recalled.
obj-2.3-source-q010.whyWrongHere: 90 seconds does not correspond to any actual LLDP default timer — LLDP's default advertisement interval is 30 seconds, and its default hold-time is 120 seconds. There is no standard LLDP timer set to 90 seconds.
obj-2.3-source-q010.memoryAnchor: LLDP's two real default numbers are 30 (timer) and 120 (hold-time) — 90 isn't a real LLDP value at all, just a guessed intermediate.
obj-2.3-source-q010.contrast: LLDP's actual default advertisement interval is 30 seconds; 90 seconds is an invented value that doesn't match either the real 30-second timer or the real 120-second hold-time.

obj-2.3-source-q010.misconceptionReason: Learners confuse LLDP's advertisement TIMER (how often frames are sent, 30 seconds) with its separate HOLD-TIME (how long a neighbor entry is kept without a refresh, 120 seconds), applying the hold-time value to the wrong question about transmit interval.
obj-2.3-source-q010.whyItSeems: Both 30 seconds and 120 seconds are genuinely correct LLDP-related numbers, just for two DIFFERENT settings — if the specific distinction between 'how often sent' (timer) versus 'how long kept' (hold-time) isn't precisely recalled, the two numbers can get swapped.
obj-2.3-source-q010.whyWrongHere: 120 seconds is LLDP's default HOLD-TIME — how long a switch retains a neighbor's LLDP information without a fresh advertisement — not the advertisement interval itself, which is 30 seconds. The question specifically asks how OFTEN frames are sent, which is the 30-second timer, not the 120-second hold-time.
obj-2.3-source-q010.memoryAnchor: 30 seconds = how OFTEN LLDP sends frames (timer); 120 seconds = how LONG a neighbor entry is kept without a refresh (hold-time) — different questions, different numbers.
obj-2.3-source-q010.contrast: The LLDP transmit timer (30 seconds) controls the frequency of outgoing advertisements; the LLDP hold-time (120 seconds) controls how long a stale entry survives without a fresh update — this question specifically asks about the shorter transmit interval.

obj-2.3-source-q011.misconceptionReason: Students think there's a single blanket 'no lldp' toggle per interface, mirroring how 'no cdp enable' works, so they type 'no lldp' expecting it to disable outbound advertisements.
obj-2.3-source-q011.whyItSeems: 'no lldp' reads like the natural negation of 'lldp' and mirrors other IOS 'no <feature>' patterns, so it feels like valid shorthand.
obj-2.3-source-q011.whyWrongHere: IOS requires the specific sub-keyword transmit or receive under the interface — LLDP direction is controlled separately so you can suppress outbound while keeping inbound (or vice versa). 'no lldp' alone is not accepted per-interface syntax; only 'no lldp transmit' turns off outgoing advertisements as the question requires.
obj-2.3-source-q011.memoryAnchor: LLDP outbound stops = no lldp transmit, not just 'no lldp.'
obj-2.3-source-q011.contrast: no lldp transmit only silences what this switch sends; no lldp receive only blocks what it listens for — they are independent switches, not one combined toggle.

obj-2.3-source-q011.misconceptionReason: Learners conflate 'stop advertising' with 'stop LLDP processing altogether,' so they pick the receive-side command believing it also halts transmission.
obj-2.3-source-q011.whyItSeems: Both transmit and receive are LLDP sub-commands with similar naming, so it's easy to grab the wrong direction under exam pressure.
obj-2.3-source-q011.whyWrongHere: no lldp receive only stops the switch from processing incoming LLDP frames — it says nothing about what this interface transmits. The question asks to stop sending, which requires no lldp transmit specifically.
obj-2.3-source-q011.memoryAnchor: receive = what you hear; transmit = what you say — disabling one doesn't touch the other.
obj-2.3-source-q011.contrast: no lldp receive leaves this switch invisible to LLDP info but still broadcasting its own; no lldp transmit does the opposite.

obj-2.3-source-q011.misconceptionReason: Students borrow 'enable' from other interface toggles (like 'cdp enable') assuming LLDP follows the identical enable/disable keyword pattern.
obj-2.3-source-q011.whyItSeems: Cisco IOS does use 'no cdp enable' for CDP, so it's a reasonable but incorrect guess that LLDP mirrors CDP's exact syntax.
obj-2.3-source-q011.whyWrongHere: LLDP's interface commands use transmit/receive directionality, not a single enable flag like CDP. 'no lldp enable' isn't valid IOS syntax; suppressing outbound requires no lldp transmit.
obj-2.3-source-q011.memoryAnchor: CDP toggles with enable; LLDP toggles with transmit/receive — different verbs, don't swap them.
obj-2.3-source-q011.contrast: cdp enable is a single on/off switch per interface; LLDP splits that switch into two independent transmit and receive controls.

obj-2.3-source-q012.misconceptionReason: Students remember '30 seconds' from LLDP material and assume it's the holdtime, when 30s is actually the transmit interval, not the aging timer.
obj-2.3-source-q012.whyItSeems: 30 seconds is genuinely an LLDP-related number (how often advertisements go out), so it feels right when the question only says 'timer.'
obj-2.3-source-q012.whyWrongHere: The transmit interval (how often LLDP sends updates) and the holdtime (how long a neighbor entry is kept before aging out) are two separate values. LLDP's default holdtime is 120 seconds, four times the 30-second interval, giving time to miss a few updates before expiring.
obj-2.3-source-q012.memoryAnchor: LLDP sends every 30s, but keeps entries for 120s — four missed messages before it forgets you.
obj-2.3-source-q012.contrast: The transmit timer controls how chatty LLDP is; the holdtime controls how patient it is before dropping a neighbor.

obj-2.3-source-q012.misconceptionReason: Learners mix up CDP's 60-second advertisement default with LLDP's holdtime, assuming the two protocols share identical timer values.
obj-2.3-source-q012.whyItSeems: CDP and LLDP are taught side by side as 'the same idea, different protocol,' so their timers blur together in memory.
obj-2.3-source-q012.whyWrongHere: CDP's default advertisement interval is 60 seconds, but that's a different protocol and a different kind of timer. LLDP's holdtime — the time before an unrefreshed neighbor entry ages out — defaults to 120 seconds.
obj-2.3-source-q012.memoryAnchor: CDP = 60s send / 180s hold. LLDP = 30s send / 120s hold. Don't cross the wires.
obj-2.3-source-q012.contrast: CDP and LLDP do the same job but keep separate clocks — matching a CDP number to an LLDP question is the trap here.

obj-2.3-source-q012.misconceptionReason: Students guess a value between the known 30-second interval and larger neighbor-discovery timers, landing on 90 seconds as a plausible-sounding middle ground.
obj-2.3-source-q012.whyItSeems: 90 seconds isn't tied to any real Cisco default the student remembers, so it functions as an 'in-between' guess when unsure.
obj-2.3-source-q012.whyWrongHere: LLDP's holdtime isn't an arbitrary middle value — it's fixed at 120 seconds by default (4x the 30-second transmit interval). There's no standard 90-second LLDP timer to fall back on.
obj-2.3-source-q012.memoryAnchor: If you're guessing a round number for LLDP holdtime, the real answer is 120 — not 90.
obj-2.3-source-q012.contrast: 120 seconds is the documented default; 90 seconds only sounds plausible because it's between two other numbers you half-remember.

obj-2.3-source-q013.misconceptionReason: Students read 'Holdtime: 162 sec' as a log timestamp — 'this was seen 162 seconds ago' — rather than as a countdown.
obj-2.3-source-q013.whyItSeems: '162 sec' next to advertisement-like output looks like an age/elapsed-time field, especially since other show commands do report 'last seen' values.
obj-2.3-source-q013.whyWrongHere: CDP's holdtime field is a countdown to expiration, not a record of elapsed time — it tells you how much longer the entry stays valid before CDP ages it out if no fresh advertisement arrives. It says nothing about when the last advertisement was received.
obj-2.3-source-q013.memoryAnchor: Holdtime counts down to deletion, it doesn't count up from receipt.
obj-2.3-source-q013.contrast: A 'last seen' field would shrink toward zero as time passes since receipt; holdtime resets to its max value every time a fresh CDP packet arrives — it's a timeout, not a clock.

obj-2.3-source-q013.misconceptionReason: Students swap the local Interface field with the neighbor's Port ID field, assuming both describe the same switch's port.
obj-2.3-source-q013.whyItSeems: Both fields list an interface name (GigabitEthernet0/x) right next to each other in the output, so it's easy to misread which one belongs to which device.
obj-2.3-source-q013.whyWrongHere: In CDP detail output, 'Interface' always names the local port receiving the advertisement (Gi0/2 here), while 'Port ID (outgoing port)' names the neighbor's port that sent it (Gi0/1 on SwitchB). So SwitchB's Gi0/1 connects out to SwitchA's Gi0/2 — not the reverse pairing this choice describes.
obj-2.3-source-q013.memoryAnchor: Interface = my port. Port ID = their port. Read outward, not inward.
obj-2.3-source-q013.contrast: Gi0/1 in the Port ID line belongs to SwitchB, the neighbor — Gi0/2 in the Interface line belongs to this switch (SwitchA) receiving the CDP frame.

obj-2.3-source-q013.misconceptionReason: Students invent an IP address (192.168.1.1) that 'feels' like a natural gateway/neighbor pairing with 192.168.1.2, rather than reading the actual output.
obj-2.3-source-q013.whyItSeems: 192.168.1.1 and 192.168.1.2 are the classic paired addresses in subnet examples, so it's tempting to assume the local device holds .1 if the neighbor holds .2.
obj-2.3-source-q013.whyWrongHere: The CDP detail output explicitly lists 'Entry address(es): IP 192.168.1.2' for SwitchB — that is SwitchB's management address, not an inferred pairing. 192.168.1.1 never appears anywhere in this output.
obj-2.3-source-q013.memoryAnchor: Only trust the IP printed in the output — don't invent a 'matching' address from habit.
obj-2.3-source-q013.contrast: 192.168.1.2 is SwitchB's documented address in the Entry address(es) field; 192.168.1.1 is a guess with no supporting line in the exhibit.

obj-2.3-source-q014.misconceptionReason: Students think there's a global 'cdp disable' command that turns off CDP capability advertising on the current interface context.
obj-2.3-source-q014.whyItSeems: 'disable' is an intuitive-sounding keyword for 'turn this off,' and IOS does use disable in some other contexts, so it seems like it should exist here too.
obj-2.3-source-q014.whyWrongHere: There is no 'cdp disable' command in Cisco IOS syntax, global or otherwise. Per-interface CDP suppression uses the negation of the enable keyword — no cdp enable — issued under the interface, not global config.
obj-2.3-source-q014.memoryAnchor: IOS turns CDP off per-port with 'no cdp enable,' not an invented 'cdp disable.'
obj-2.3-source-q014.contrast: Global config (config)# has no CDP disable command; interface config (config-if)# no cdp enable is the actual syntax that stops advertisements on one port.

obj-2.3-source-q014.misconceptionReason: Students assume 'no cdp' alone is a complete, valid command, treating CDP like a single monolithic feature you can just negate outright.
obj-2.3-source-q014.whyItSeems: 'no <protocol-name>' is a common IOS pattern for disabling many features, so dropping the 'enable' keyword seems like harmless shorthand.
obj-2.3-source-q014.whyWrongHere: CDP's per-interface toggle requires the full keyword — enable — after cdp. 'no cdp' by itself is incomplete interface syntax and won't stop advertisements the way the scenario requires; the actual command is no cdp enable.
obj-2.3-source-q014.memoryAnchor: CDP's interface switch has a name: 'enable.' Leaving it off leaves the command incomplete.
obj-2.3-source-q014.contrast: no cdp enable is a complete, valid per-interface command; no cdp on its own is not recognized syntax for suppressing CDP on that port.

obj-2.3-source-q014.misconceptionReason: Students think negating 'disable' is the way to disable something, applying a double-negative logic that doesn't map onto how this command actually works.
obj-2.3-source-q014.whyItSeems: 'no cdp disable' sounds like it should mean 'make sure CDP stays disabled,' following an intuitive (but backwards) reading of double negatives.
obj-2.3-source-q014.whyWrongHere: 'no cdp disable' would only make sense if 'cdp disable' were valid syntax to begin with (it isn't) — and even then, negating it would re-enable rather than suppress CDP. To selectively stop CDP advertisements on the ISP-facing interface, the correct command is no cdp enable.
obj-2.3-source-q014.memoryAnchor: Don't chase double negatives — the real command is a single negation: no cdp enable.
obj-2.3-source-q014.contrast: no cdp enable directly turns off advertising on this port; no cdp disable is a nonsense combination built on a command that was never valid.

obj-2.3-source-q015.misconceptionReason: Students think 'show cdp' alone already reports which interfaces have CDP enabled, since it sounds like the general CDP status command.
obj-2.3-source-q015.whyItSeems: 'show cdp' is a real, valid command, so it's tempting to assume it covers interface-level detail too, especially since it's shorter and easier to remember.
obj-2.3-source-q015.whyWrongHere: show cdp (without arguments) reports global CDP timers and version — it does not list per-interface CDP status. To see which interfaces are actively advertising CDP, you need the more specific show cdp interface.
obj-2.3-source-q015.memoryAnchor: show cdp = global settings. show cdp interface = which ports are talking.
obj-2.3-source-q015.contrast: show cdp gives you the protocol's global timers; show cdp interface gives you the per-port picture the question actually asks for.

obj-2.3-source-q015.misconceptionReason: Students reach for the generic show interface command because it's the most familiar way to check interface status, forgetting it isn't protocol-specific.
obj-2.3-source-q015.whyItSeems: show interface is the workhorse command for interface state, so it feels like a safe default answer for any 'which interfaces...' question.
obj-2.3-source-q015.whyWrongHere: show interface reports Layer 1/2 statistics (speed, duplex, counters) — it has no CDP-specific information at all. Seeing which interfaces are advertising CDP requires the CDP-specific command, show cdp interface.
obj-2.3-source-q015.memoryAnchor: Generic show interface ≠ protocol-specific show cdp interface — CDP needs its own keyword.
obj-2.3-source-q015.contrast: show interface tells you about the wire (up/down, speed, duplex); show cdp interface tells you specifically which ports are running CDP.

obj-2.3-source-q015.misconceptionReason: Students remember the two keywords 'cdp' and 'interface' but reverse their order, assuming word order doesn't matter in IOS syntax.
obj-2.3-source-q015.whyItSeems: Both keywords are correct individually, so swapping their order feels like a minor, inconsequential mistake rather than an invalid command.
obj-2.3-source-q015.whyWrongHere: IOS command syntax is order-sensitive — show interface cdp is not a recognized command. The valid form places the protocol keyword first: show cdp interface.
obj-2.3-source-q015.memoryAnchor: Keyword order matters in IOS: it's 'show cdp interface,' never 'show interface cdp.'
obj-2.3-source-q015.contrast: show cdp interface is valid, documented syntax; reversing it to show interface cdp produces an unrecognized command on real hardware.

obj-2.4-source-q001.misconceptionReason: Students recall that at least two links are needed to form an EtherChannel and mistakenly treat that minimum as also being the maximum.
obj-2.4-source-q001.whyItSeems: EtherChannel is introduced as 'bundling 2+ links,' so it's easy to fixate on the number 2 as the defining limit rather than just the starting point.
obj-2.4-source-q001.whyWrongHere: Two is simply the minimum number of physical ports needed to form a channel — it's not a ceiling. PAgP specifically allows bundling up to 8 active interfaces into one logical link.
obj-2.4-source-q001.memoryAnchor: 2 is where EtherChannel starts, not where it stops — PAgP tops out at 8.
obj-2.4-source-q001.contrast: The minimum bundle size (2) and the maximum bundle size (8) are two different numbers; this question asks specifically for the maximum.

obj-2.4-source-q001.misconceptionReason: Students confuse PAgP's limit with LACP's 16-interface total (8 active + 8 standby), assuming both protocols share the same maximum.
obj-2.4-source-q001.whyItSeems: 16 is a real EtherChannel-related number — it's just tied to LACP's standby feature, not PAgP, so it's a plausible-sounding mix-up.
obj-2.4-source-q001.whyWrongHere: LACP supports up to 16 total interfaces per channel (8 active plus 8 in hot-standby), but PAgP has no standby mechanism — its maximum is simply 8 active interfaces.
obj-2.4-source-q001.memoryAnchor: LACP has a bench (16 = 8 active + 8 standby); PAgP doesn't — PAgP caps at 8.
obj-2.4-source-q001.contrast: 16 belongs to LACP's active+standby model; PAgP bundles a flat maximum of 8 active links with no reserve pool.

obj-2.4-source-q001.misconceptionReason: Students recall 4 as a round, 'safe-sounding' EtherChannel number, possibly confusing it with common lab examples that only ever bundle 2-4 ports.
obj-2.4-source-q001.whyItSeems: Many training labs demonstrate EtherChannel with just 2-4 links for simplicity, so learners may mistake the example size for the protocol's actual ceiling.
obj-2.4-source-q001.whyWrongHere: Four links is a valid (and common) bundle size in practice, but it is not PAgP's maximum. PAgP supports up to 8 active interfaces in a single channel group.
obj-2.4-source-q001.memoryAnchor: Lab examples often use 4 links for simplicity — that's a convenience, not PAgP's actual 8-link ceiling.
obj-2.4-source-q001.contrast: 4 is a commonly demonstrated bundle size; 8 is PAgP's documented architectural maximum — don't mistake a teaching example for a hard limit.

obj-2.4-source-q002.misconceptionReason: Students blend STP's 'block redundant links' behavior with EtherChannel, assuming EtherChannel needs 802.1Q blocking to prevent loops the way STP does.
obj-2.4-source-q002.whyItSeems: Both EtherChannel and 802.1Q/STP deal with 'avoiding problems from redundant links,' so it's easy to merge the two mechanisms into one imagined feature.
obj-2.4-source-q002.whyWrongHere: EtherChannel doesn't need 802.1Q to block anything — bundling the physical links into one logical interface is what prevents STP from seeing redundant paths in the first place. 802.1Q handles VLAN tagging on trunk links, an entirely separate function.
obj-2.4-source-q002.memoryAnchor: EtherChannel prevents the loop by merging links, not by asking 802.1Q to block one.
obj-2.4-source-q002.contrast: 802.1Q tags VLANs across a trunk; EtherChannel bundles physical ports into one logical link so STP has nothing redundant left to block.

obj-2.4-source-q002.misconceptionReason: Students assume EtherChannel is flexible enough to bundle any mismatched links together, since 'aggregation' sounds like it should tolerate different speeds.
obj-2.4-source-q002.whyItSeems: The word 'aggregate' suggests combining diverse resources, so mixing speeds feels like a natural extension of the aggregation idea.
obj-2.4-source-q002.whyWrongHere: All member links in an EtherChannel bundle must match speed and duplex — mismatched links won't bundle successfully. EtherChannel's defining behavior is instead that it presents the group as one single logical Layer 2 connection.
obj-2.4-source-q002.memoryAnchor: Aggregation still demands uniformity: same speed, same duplex, every member port.
obj-2.4-source-q002.contrast: Aggregating traffic across links is not the same as tolerating varying speeds — EtherChannel requires identical link parameters even while combining bandwidth.

obj-2.4-source-q002.misconceptionReason: Students imagine EtherChannel as flexible enough to span multiple independent, unstacked switches, treating 'aggregation' as if it works across any physical boundary.
obj-2.4-source-q002.whyItSeems: Technologies like StackWise or vPC do let you bundle across chassis, so it's easy to assume plain EtherChannel works the same way.
obj-2.4-source-q002.whyWrongHere: A standard EtherChannel bundles physical ports on the same switch (or the same logical stack/VSS pair) into one logical interface — it can't span two genuinely standalone switches without a special cross-chassis technology like vPC or StackWise. What's actually true about EtherChannel is that it behaves as a single Layer 2 connection once formed.
obj-2.4-source-q002.memoryAnchor: Plain EtherChannel bundles ports on one switch; crossing standalone switches needs vPC/VSS/StackWise, not vanilla EtherChannel.
obj-2.4-source-q002.contrast: vPC/StackWise are the technologies that extend bundling across separate chassis; EtherChannel by itself assumes the member ports live on the same switching entity.

obj-2.4-source-q003.misconceptionReason: Students try to combine some FastEthernet capacity with the gigabit ports, assuming EtherChannel can blend different port speeds into one bundle to squeeze out extra bandwidth.
obj-2.4-source-q003.whyItSeems: 'Aggregation' implies adding capacity together, so mixing 2 Gb/s worth of gigabit ports with a bit of FastEthernet feels like it should yield something above a clean 2 Gb/s.
obj-2.4-source-q003.whyWrongHere: EtherChannel requires every member port to match speed and duplex — you cannot combine FastEthernet and Gigabit ports in the same channel group. The only compatible pair here is the two gigabit ports, giving exactly 2 Gb/s, not a blended figure like 2.2 Gb/s.
obj-2.4-source-q003.memoryAnchor: You can't blend speeds into one bundle — matching ports only, so it's a clean 2 Gb/s, not a fractional mix.
obj-2.4-source-q003.contrast: 2 Gb/s comes from bundling two identical gigabit ports; 2.2 Gb/s would require mixing speeds, which EtherChannel simply does not allow.

obj-2.4-source-q003.misconceptionReason: Students only consider the FastEthernet ports (bundling some subset of the 48) and ignore the higher-capacity gigabit ports entirely, undercounting the best possible bandwidth.
obj-2.4-source-q003.whyItSeems: With 48 FastEthernet ports available, it's tempting to focus on that larger pool and calculate a FastEthernet-only bundle (e.g., 4 x 100 Mb/s = 400 Mb/s) as 'the' answer.
obj-2.4-source-q003.whyWrongHere: The question asks for the highest achievable bandwidth, and the two gigabit ports alone bundle to 2 Gb/s — far higher than any all-FastEthernet combination. Since PAgP requires matching speeds, the best strategy is bundling the gigabit pair, not the FastEthernet ports.
obj-2.4-source-q003.memoryAnchor: For 'highest bandwidth,' always check whether faster ports exist before defaulting to the larger pool of slower ones.
obj-2.4-source-q003.contrast: 400 Mb/s comes from a FastEthernet-only bundle; 2 Gb/s comes from the gigabit pair — the gigabit option wins for maximum throughput.

obj-2.4-source-q003.misconceptionReason: Students add the two gigabit ports' 2 Gb/s to some FastEthernet capacity (e.g., 6 x 100 Mb/s), assuming EtherChannel bundles can freely mix and sum speeds.
obj-2.4-source-q003.whyItSeems: Arithmetic addition of 'available bandwidth' feels natural if you don't apply the matching-speed constraint, especially with so many FastEthernet ports sitting unused.
obj-2.4-source-q003.whyWrongHere: EtherChannel members must share the same speed and duplex settings — the gigabit ports and FastEthernet ports cannot join the same channel group, so their bandwidths can never be summed together. The maximum achievable is 2 Gb/s from the two matching gigabit ports alone.
obj-2.4-source-q003.memoryAnchor: No mixing means no adding — different-speed ports never combine into one channel's bandwidth total.
obj-2.4-source-q003.contrast: 2.6 Gb/s assumes cross-speed bundling is allowed; 2 Gb/s reflects the real constraint that only same-speed ports can join one EtherChannel.

obj-2.4-source-q004.misconceptionReason: Students recognize 802.1Q as an IEEE standard and, without checking what it actually covers, assume it must be the aggregation-related one being asked about.
obj-2.4-source-q004.whyItSeems: 802.1Q is a genuine, commonly-tested IEEE standard in the same general 'switching' topic area, so it's easy to misattribute it to link aggregation.
obj-2.4-source-q004.whyWrongHere: 802.1Q defines VLAN trunk tagging — how frames carry VLAN information across a trunk link — not link aggregation negotiation. The IEEE standard for bundling multiple links is LACP (802.3ad).
obj-2.4-source-q004.memoryAnchor: 802.1Q tags VLANs on a trunk; LACP (802.3ad) bundles links — different jobs, both IEEE.
obj-2.4-source-q004.contrast: 802.1Q solves 'how do multiple VLANs share one trunk'; LACP solves 'how do multiple physical links act as one logical link' — unrelated problems.

obj-2.4-source-q004.misconceptionReason: Students know PAgP does the same job as LACP (link aggregation negotiation) and assume that because it's a real Cisco protocol, it must also be the IEEE standard.
obj-2.4-source-q004.whyItSeems: PAgP and LACP accomplish the identical task, so without a clear memory of 'who owns which,' it's a coin-flip guess between the two.
obj-2.4-source-q004.whyWrongHere: PAgP (Port Aggregation Protocol) is Cisco-proprietary — it only works between Cisco devices. The IEEE open standard covering the same function is LACP, standardized as 802.3ad.
obj-2.4-source-q004.contrast: PAgP negotiates bundles only between Cisco switches; LACP negotiates bundles between any vendor's equipment because it's an open IEEE standard.

obj-2.4-source-q004.misconceptionReason: Students recall 802.1X as an IEEE networking standard and mistakenly slot it into the 'aggregation protocol' category simply because it's also an 802.1-series number.
obj-2.4-source-q004.whyItSeems: The similar numbering (802.1X vs. 802.3ad) can blur together for students who haven't cleanly separated the different 802-series standards by function.
obj-2.4-source-q004.whyWrongHere: 802.1X governs port-based network access control (authentication before a port is allowed to pass traffic) — it has nothing to do with combining multiple physical links. The aggregation standard is LACP, IEEE 802.3ad.
obj-2.4-source-q004.memoryAnchor: 802.1X gates who gets on the network; LACP (802.3ad) bundles the links once you're already on it — completely different concerns.
obj-2.4-source-q004.contrast: 802.1X is about authentication and access control; LACP is about link aggregation — sharing a numbering prefix doesn't mean sharing a function.

obj-2.4-source-q005.misconceptionReason: Students answer with the feature's overall name because it's the term they associate most strongly with 'bundling links,' without distinguishing the feature from the negotiation protocol running underneath it.
obj-2.4-source-q005.whyItSeems: 'EtherChannel' is the word used constantly in casual discussion of link bundling, so it feels like a safe, general-purpose answer to any related question.
obj-2.4-source-q005.whyWrongHere: 'EtherChannel' is Cisco's brand name for the bundled-link feature itself — it isn't a negotiation protocol you select. The question specifically asks which protocol to choose for interoperating with a non-Cisco host, which requires naming LACP or PAgP explicitly; LACP is the one that works with third-party devices like ESXi.
obj-2.4-source-q005.memoryAnchor: 'EtherChannel' names the feature; 'LACP' or 'PAgP' name the protocol running it — pick a protocol, not the brand.
obj-2.4-source-q005.contrast: EtherChannel is the umbrella term for any bundled link; LACP is the specific negotiation protocol you must configure to make that bundle interoperate with non-Cisco gear.

obj-2.4-source-q005.misconceptionReason: Students substitute the interface configuration term ('channel-group') for an actual negotiation protocol, conflating IOS command syntax with the underlying protocol choice.
obj-2.4-source-q005.whyItSeems: 'channel-group' is the command keyword used to bundle interfaces in IOS, so it's easy to mistake it for the protocol name itself.
obj-2.4-source-q005.whyWrongHere: 'Channel Group' describes the logical interface bundle configuration construct in IOS — it isn't a negotiation protocol. For a non-Cisco device like an ESXi host, you must choose the IEEE-standard protocol, LACP.
obj-2.4-source-q005.memoryAnchor: Channel-group is the container command; LACP/PAgP is what negotiates inside it.
obj-2.4-source-q005.contrast: The channel-group command creates the bundle interface; LACP or PAgP is the protocol you specify as a mode within that command — they operate at different levels.

obj-2.4-source-q005.misconceptionReason: Students assume any Cisco-side EtherChannel negotiation defaults to PAgP without considering that the far-end device (ESXi) isn't a Cisco switch.
obj-2.4-source-q005.whyItSeems: PAgP is a familiar, commonly taught EtherChannel protocol, so it's a natural first guess if the vendor-compatibility detail in the scenario is overlooked.
obj-2.4-source-q005.whyWrongHere: PAgP (Port Aggregation Protocol) is Cisco-proprietary and won't negotiate successfully with a non-Cisco host like a VMware ESXi server. For interoperability with third-party devices, you must use LACP, the IEEE 802.3ad open standard.
obj-2.4-source-q005.memoryAnchor: Talking to non-Cisco gear? PAgP won't understand you — only LACP speaks the open standard.
obj-2.4-source-q005.contrast: PAgP only negotiates between Cisco devices; LACP negotiates between any vendor's equipment, which is exactly what an ESXi-to-switch bundle requires.

obj-2.4-source-q006.misconceptionReason: Students confuse the minimum number of ports needed to start a bundle with LACP's actual upper limit.
obj-2.4-source-q006.whyItSeems: Two is the smallest number that still counts as 'aggregation,' so it lingers in memory as if it were a defining ceiling rather than just a starting point.
obj-2.4-source-q006.whyWrongHere: Two links form the smallest possible EtherChannel, but LACP's maximum bundle size is far larger — up to 16 total interfaces (8 active plus 8 standby).
obj-2.4-source-q006.memoryAnchor: 2 is the floor for any EtherChannel; 16 is LACP's actual ceiling.
obj-2.4-source-q006.contrast: The minimum needed to call it a bundle (2) and LACP's maximum supported size (16) are entirely different numbers — this question asks for the maximum.

obj-2.4-source-q006.misconceptionReason: Students recall '8' as an EtherChannel-related number but apply PAgP's active-only maximum to LACP, missing that LACP also supports a standby pool.
obj-2.4-source-q006.whyItSeems: 8 is genuinely the number of active links LACP can carry simultaneously, so stopping there without accounting for standby ports produces a plausible but incomplete answer.
obj-2.4-source-q006.whyWrongHere: LACP does cap active forwarding links at 8, but it can also hold up to 8 additional interfaces in hot-standby, ready to take over if an active link fails — bringing the total configurable maximum to 16.
obj-2.4-source-q006.memoryAnchor: 8 active + 8 standby = 16 total under LACP — don't stop counting at the active-only number.
obj-2.4-source-q006.contrast: 8 is the maximum number of links LACP will actively forward on simultaneously; 16 is the maximum total interfaces you can assign to the group, counting the standby pool.

obj-2.4-source-q006.misconceptionReason: Students recall a small, 'textbook example' bundle size from a lab or diagram and mistake that illustrative number for LACP's actual architectural limit.
obj-2.4-source-q006.whyItSeems: Many demonstrations only bundle a handful of ports for simplicity, so 4 can feel like a familiar, safe-sounding ceiling.
obj-2.4-source-q006.whyWrongHere: Four links is a common example size, not a protocol limit. LACP's actual supported maximum is 16 total interfaces (8 active, 8 standby).
obj-2.4-source-q006.memoryAnchor: A 4-port example in a lab diagram is not the same as LACP's real 16-interface maximum.
obj-2.4-source-q006.contrast: 4 might be what a training scenario shows for simplicity; 16 is the actual number Cisco documents as LACP's supported maximum.

obj-2.4-source-q007.misconceptionReason: Students invent a nonexistent 'off mode' for LACP, assuming every protocol must have a matching 'off' keyword the way it has 'on.'
obj-2.4-source-q007.whyItSeems: The word 'off' pairs naturally with 'on' in everyday language, making 'LACP off mode' sound like a real configuration option even though it isn't part of Cisco's actual mode set.
obj-2.4-source-q007.whyWrongHere: LACP's real modes are active and passive — there is no 'off' keyword. The mode that forces a bundle without running any control protocol at all is simply channel-group mode on, which bypasses LACP entirely rather than being a variant of it.
obj-2.4-source-q007.memoryAnchor: LACP's real modes are active/passive — 'on' isn't an LACP mode at all, it replaces LACP entirely.
obj-2.4-source-q007.contrast: LACP active/passive still negotiates using LACP packets; on mode skips LACP negotiation altogether and just forces the link up.

obj-2.4-source-q007.misconceptionReason: Students similarly invent an 'off' variant for PAgP, assuming its real modes (desirable/auto) must also include an off setting.
obj-2.4-source-q007.whyItSeems: Because PAgP has two named modes already (desirable, auto), adding a third 'off' mode feels like filling in a natural gap in the pattern.
obj-2.4-source-q007.whyWrongHere: PAgP's actual modes are desirable and auto — there's no 'off' mode within PAgP. Forcing a bundle without negotiation at all uses the separate on mode, which doesn't use PAgP (or LACP) at all.
obj-2.4-source-q007.memoryAnchor: PAgP's real modes are desirable/auto — 'on' mode isn't PAgP running quietly, it's no protocol running at all.
obj-2.4-source-q007.contrast: PAgP desirable/auto still exchange PAgP hello packets; on mode sends none — it's a completely different, protocol-free path to forming the channel.

obj-2.4-source-q007.misconceptionReason: Students equate 'no control protocol' with 'the open standard protocol,' mistakenly treating 802.3ad (LACP) as if it were the unconditional, negotiation-free option.
obj-2.4-source-q007.whyItSeems: 802.3ad is a formal-sounding IEEE designation, so it can be mistaken for a special 'guaranteed' or 'forced' mode rather than recognized as simply another name for LACP.
obj-2.4-source-q007.whyWrongHere: 802.3ad is the IEEE standard name for LACP — it still requires active/passive negotiation between switches, just like any LACP configuration. The mode that skips negotiation entirely is on mode, a separate mechanism from both LACP (802.3ad) and PAgP.
obj-2.4-source-q007.memoryAnchor: 802.3ad is just another name for LACP — it still negotiates. Only 'on' mode skips negotiation.
obj-2.4-source-q007.contrast: 802.3ad/LACP exchanges control packets to agree on the bundle; on mode statically forces the bundle with zero control-protocol exchange.

obj-2.4-source-q008.misconceptionReason: Students assume any EtherChannel negotiation protocol should interoperate broadly across vendors, not realizing PAgP specifically is locked to Cisco equipment.
obj-2.4-source-q008.whyItSeems: PAgP sounds like a generic 'port aggregation' name without an obvious vendor marker, so nothing about the name itself signals it's proprietary.
obj-2.4-source-q008.whyWrongHere: PAgP is Cisco-proprietary and will not negotiate with non-Cisco switches or hosts — only the IEEE-standard LACP is designed for multi-vendor interoperability. What's actually true is that 'EtherChannel' itself is Cisco's proprietary branding for the bundling feature.
obj-2.4-source-q008.memoryAnchor: PAgP only speaks to other Cisco gear — cross-vendor bundling needs LACP.
obj-2.4-source-q008.contrast: PAgP is restricted to Cisco-to-Cisco negotiation; LACP (802.3ad) is the open standard that works with non-Cisco products.

obj-2.4-source-q008.misconceptionReason: Students assume LACP, because it's discussed alongside the Cisco-specific PAgP, must also be a Cisco-only technology.
obj-2.4-source-q008.whyItSeems: LACP and PAgP are taught together as 'the two EtherChannel protocols,' so without a clear distinction, students can misattribute Cisco-exclusivity to both.
obj-2.4-source-q008.whyWrongHere: LACP (802.3ad) is an open IEEE standard specifically designed to work across vendors — it is not Cisco-only. PAgP is the one restricted to Cisco equipment; separately, 'EtherChannel' itself is Cisco's proprietary name for the bundling feature.
obj-2.4-source-q008.memoryAnchor: LACP is IEEE-open (any vendor); PAgP is Cisco-only — don't swap which one is restricted.
obj-2.4-source-q008.contrast: LACP works between a Cisco switch and, say, a Linux server or ESXi host; PAgP will only negotiate between two Cisco devices.

obj-2.4-source-q008.misconceptionReason: Students think 'aggregation' implies flexibility to combine mismatched links, assuming PAgP specifically supports bundling ports of different speeds and duplex settings.
obj-2.4-source-q008.whyItSeems: The general idea of 'aggregating' bandwidth sounds like it should tolerate some variation, especially if a student hasn't internalized the strict matching requirement.
obj-2.4-source-q008.whyWrongHere: PAgP (like LACP) requires every bundled port to match speed and duplex — mixed-speed links cannot join the same channel group under either protocol. What's actually true is that 'EtherChannel' is simply Cisco's proprietary name for the whole bundling technology.
obj-2.4-source-q008.memoryAnchor: Neither PAgP nor LACP tolerates mixed speeds — matching ports only, always.
obj-2.4-source-q008.contrast: PAgP's negotiation flexibility is about desirable/auto handshaking, not about tolerating mismatched port speeds — that requirement never relaxes.

obj-2.4-source-q009.misconceptionReason: Students reverse which protocol is proprietary, believing LACP — because it's discussed as 'the other EtherChannel option' — must be the Cisco-only one.
obj-2.4-source-q009.whyItSeems: Without a strong anchor for which protocol belongs to which camp, LACP and PAgP can feel interchangeable, making the proprietary label a coin-flip.
obj-2.4-source-q009.whyWrongHere: LACP (802.3ad) is the IEEE open standard, usable with any vendor's equipment. The Cisco-proprietary negotiation protocol is PAgP.
obj-2.4-source-q009.memoryAnchor: If it's IEEE-numbered (802.3ad), it's open — LACP is open, PAgP is Cisco's own.
obj-2.4-source-q009.contrast: LACP interoperates with any vendor because it's an open standard; PAgP only works between two Cisco devices.

obj-2.4-source-q009.misconceptionReason: Students grab a familiar 802.1-numbered standard they associate with switching in general, without checking that it actually addresses VLAN trunking, not link aggregation negotiation.
obj-2.4-source-q009.whyItSeems: 802.1Q is a well-known IEEE number in the same broad switching topic area, so it's an easy but mismatched pull for 'which protocol is Cisco-proprietary.'
obj-2.4-source-q009.whyWrongHere: 802.1Q defines VLAN trunk tagging and, being an IEEE standard, is open, not Cisco-proprietary. It also has nothing to do with EtherChannel negotiation. The proprietary EtherChannel negotiation protocol is PAgP.
obj-2.4-source-q009.memoryAnchor: 802.1Q tags VLANs on trunks — it's not even in the EtherChannel conversation, proprietary or not.
obj-2.4-source-q009.contrast: 802.1Q is an open VLAN tagging standard used on trunk links; PAgP is Cisco's proprietary protocol for negotiating link bundles — different function, different ownership.

obj-2.4-source-q009.misconceptionReason: Students recognize 802.1ab as a real IEEE standard number and guess it applies here, without knowing it's actually the LLDP specification, unrelated to link aggregation.
obj-2.4-source-q009.whyItSeems: An unfamiliar-but-official-sounding IEEE number can feel like a 'safe,' technical-sounding choice when the real answer (PAgP) isn't an IEEE number at all.
obj-2.4-source-q009.whyWrongHere: 802.1ab is the IEEE standard for LLDP, a neighbor-discovery protocol — it has nothing to do with EtherChannel negotiation. The Cisco-proprietary EtherChannel negotiation protocol is PAgP.
obj-2.4-source-q009.memoryAnchor: 802.1ab = LLDP (discovery). PAgP = EtherChannel (bundling). Don't let the IEEE number stand in for the wrong protocol.
obj-2.4-source-q009.contrast: 802.1ab governs neighbor discovery advertisements (LLDP); PAgP governs whether and how physical links bundle into an EtherChannel — unrelated protocols solving unrelated problems.

obj-2.4-source-q010.misconceptionReason: Students substitute CDP's 60-second advertisement interval for PAgP's timer, assuming all Cisco discovery/negotiation protocols share the same default cadence.
obj-2.4-source-q010.whyItSeems: 60 seconds is a real Cisco default elsewhere (CDP advertisements), so it's an easy but mismatched number to recall under exam pressure.
obj-2.4-source-q010.whyWrongHere: CDP's default interval is 60 seconds, but PAgP is a separate protocol with its own timer — it sends control messages every 30 seconds to monitor bundle link status.
obj-2.4-source-q010.memoryAnchor: CDP talks every 60s; PAgP talks every 30s — different protocols, different clocks.
obj-2.4-source-q010.contrast: 60 seconds is CDP's advertisement interval; 30 seconds is PAgP's actual message interval — don't let one protocol's timer bleed into another's question.

obj-2.4-source-q010.misconceptionReason: Students guess a number that 'sounds like' a longer Cisco timeout value without a specific memory anchor, landing on 90 seconds as a plausible middle-ground guess.
obj-2.4-source-q010.whyItSeems: 90 seconds doesn't map to any well-known Cisco default the student has memorized, so it functions as an unanchored guess rather than a documented value.
obj-2.4-source-q010.whyWrongHere: There's no standard 90-second PAgP timer — PAgP's actual message interval for monitoring bundled links is 30 seconds.
obj-2.4-source-q010.memoryAnchor: If a PAgP timer question feels like a guess, the documented answer is 30 seconds — not an in-between number like 90.
obj-2.4-source-q010.contrast: 30 seconds is PAgP's actual, documented control-message interval; 90 seconds has no basis in Cisco's PAgP timers.

obj-2.4-source-q010.misconceptionReason: Students confuse PAgP's message interval with a holdtime/aging-style timer (like LLDP's 120-second holdtime), assuming all 'protocol timers' default to the same larger value.
obj-2.4-source-q010.whyItSeems: 120 seconds is a real Cisco networking timer (LLDP holdtime), so it can surface as a plausible but misapplied answer.
obj-2.4-source-q010.whyWrongHere: 120 seconds belongs to a different protocol's aging timer (like LLDP holdtime) — it is far too slow for PAgP's actual behavior, which sends control messages every 30 seconds to keep bundle status current.
obj-2.4-source-q010.memoryAnchor: 120 seconds is someone else's holdtime (LLDP); PAgP's own message cadence is 30 seconds.
obj-2.4-source-q010.contrast: 120 seconds describes how long a neighbor entry is kept before aging out in other protocols; 30 seconds describes how often PAgP itself sends control messages — these are different kinds of timers entirely.

obj-2.4-source-q011.misconceptionReason: Students think any matching pair of modes on both sides will successfully negotiate LACP, without realizing passive ports never initiate.
obj-2.4-source-q011.whyItSeems: 'Matching modes' (both sides configured identically) sounds like the safe, symmetric choice, so passive/passive can feel just as valid as active/active.
obj-2.4-source-q011.whyWrongHere: LACP passive mode means 'wait and respond, never initiate.' If both sides are passive, neither one ever sends the first LACP packet, so no negotiation happens and the channel never forms. At least one side (or both) must be active to force LACP to actually start.
obj-2.4-source-q011.memoryAnchor: Passive waits forever for someone else to speak first — two passives means silence forever.
obj-2.4-source-q011.contrast: Active/active guarantees negotiation starts immediately; passive/passive guarantees it never starts at all.

obj-2.4-source-q011.misconceptionReason: Students mix up PAgP's mode vocabulary (auto/desirable) with LACP's (active/passive), assuming 'auto' is a valid LACP setting.
obj-2.4-source-q011.whyItSeems: Auto and active/passive are both 'mode keywords' taught in the same EtherChannel lesson, so it's easy to blur which vocabulary belongs to which protocol.
obj-2.4-source-q011.whyWrongHere: 'Auto' is a PAgP-only mode — it doesn't exist for LACP. To force LACP specifically, both sides need the LACP-specific keyword active (or one active, one passive).
obj-2.4-source-q011.memoryAnchor: Auto/desirable = PAgP's words. Active/passive = LACP's words. Keep the vocabularies separate.
obj-2.4-source-q011.contrast: Auto mode belongs to PAgP's desirable/auto negotiation scheme; active mode belongs to LACP's active/passive scheme — the question specifically asks about forcing LACP.

obj-2.4-source-q011.misconceptionReason: Students again cross PAgP's mode vocabulary into an LACP question, assuming 'desirable' (which does actively initiate negotiation in PAgP) is also valid for LACP.
obj-2.4-source-q011.whyItSeems: Desirable mode does actively start negotiation in PAgP, which mirrors what 'active' does in LACP — so students borrow the word without switching protocol families.
obj-2.4-source-q011.whyWrongHere: Desirable is a PAgP-only mode; it isn't part of LACP's keyword set at all. To specifically use LACP (as the scenario asks), you must configure active mode (IEEE 802.3ad terminology), not PAgP's desirable.
obj-2.4-source-q011.memoryAnchor: Desirable belongs to PAgP; active belongs to LACP — matching behavior doesn't mean matching keyword.
obj-2.4-source-q011.contrast: Desirable is how you actively initiate a PAgP bundle; active is how you actively initiate an LACP bundle — same intent, different protocol, different required keyword.

obj-2.4-source-q012.misconceptionReason: Students see the word 'channel group' forming and default to naming PAgP, since it may be the first EtherChannel protocol they memorized, without checking that active/passive are LACP-specific keywords.
obj-2.4-source-q012.whyItSeems: PAgP and LACP are often studied as interchangeable 'EtherChannel protocols,' so naming either one can feel equally safe without paying attention to the mode keywords given.
obj-2.4-source-q012.whyWrongHere: Active and passive are LACP's mode keywords specifically — PAgP uses desirable and auto instead. Since the scenario specifies active/passive, the channel that forms is necessarily LACP, not PAgP.
obj-2.4-source-q012.memoryAnchor: See 'active/passive' → think LACP. See 'desirable/auto' → think PAgP.
obj-2.4-source-q012.contrast: PAgP negotiates using desirable and auto; this scenario's active/passive pairing is LACP's vocabulary, so LACP — not PAgP — is what actually forms.

obj-2.4-source-q012.misconceptionReason: Students overgeneralize from the passive/passive failure case, assuming any pairing that includes 'passive' at all must fail to negotiate.
obj-2.4-source-q012.whyItSeems: Because passive/passive famously fails to form a channel, it's easy to assume passive is somehow 'risky' in any combination, including with active.
obj-2.4-source-q012.whyWrongHere: LACP only fails to negotiate when both sides are passive (neither initiates). Pairing one active side with one passive side works fine — the active side initiates, and the passive side responds, successfully forming an LACP channel.
obj-2.4-source-q012.memoryAnchor: Passive alone doesn't block negotiation — passive plus passive does. One active side is enough to start things.
obj-2.4-source-q012.contrast: Passive+passive = no initiator, no channel; active+passive = one initiator, one responder, a channel forms successfully.

obj-2.4-source-q012.misconceptionReason: Students answer with the general feature name instead of the specific negotiation protocol, since 'EtherChannel' is the umbrella term they're most comfortable with.
obj-2.4-source-q012.whyItSeems: 'EtherChannel' technically describes what results (a bundled link), so it feels like a reasonable, safe answer even though it doesn't name the protocol the question is asking about.
obj-2.4-source-q012.whyWrongHere: The question specifically asks which protocol negotiates the channel given these active/passive keywords — those keywords belong to LACP specifically. 'EtherChannel' is the resulting feature, not the protocol answer being tested.
obj-2.4-source-q012.memoryAnchor: EtherChannel is the noun for the result; LACP is the protocol that got you there — the question wants the protocol.
obj-2.4-source-q012.contrast: EtherChannel describes any bundled logical link, regardless of protocol; LACP is the specific protocol identified by the active/passive mode keywords in this scenario.

obj-2.4-source-q013.misconceptionReason: Students invent an incomplete command by remembering just the 'port-channel' keyword without its required qualifier, assuming it stands alone as a full show command.
obj-2.4-source-q013.whyItSeems: 'port-channel' is the interface type name shown throughout EtherChannel configuration, so it feels natural to expect a matching bare show command.
obj-2.4-source-q013.whyWrongHere: 'show port-channel' by itself is not valid/complete IOS syntax for this purpose — you need show etherchannel (optionally with summary or detail) to see the negotiated protocol and port states.
obj-2.4-source-q013.memoryAnchor: The verification keyword is 'etherchannel,' not 'port-channel' — even though the interface itself is named Port-channelX.
obj-2.4-source-q013.contrast: 'Port-channel' names the logical interface object; 'show etherchannel' is the actual command family used to verify its negotiated protocol and status.

obj-2.4-source-q013.misconceptionReason: Students default to the generic interface-status command because it's the most familiar tool for checking any interface, without considering that it lacks EtherChannel-protocol detail.
obj-2.4-source-q013.whyItSeems: show interface is genuinely useful for checking Port-channel interface up/down state, so it's a plausible-sounding (if incomplete) guess.
obj-2.4-source-q013.whyWrongHere: show interface reports Layer 1/2 statistics and status for an interface (including a Port-channel interface), but it does not report which negotiation protocol (LACP or PAgP) is in use — that specific detail comes from show etherchannel.
obj-2.4-source-q013.memoryAnchor: show interface tells you if the bundle is up; show etherchannel tells you how it was negotiated.
obj-2.4-source-q013.contrast: show interface covers general up/down and traffic counters; show etherchannel specifically reveals the negotiation protocol and per-port channel state.

obj-2.4-source-q013.misconceptionReason: Students think reading the configuration text will directly reveal the negotiated protocol, confusing 'what was configured' with 'what actually negotiated.'
obj-2.4-source-q013.whyItSeems: show run does display the configured mode keyword (active, passive, desirable, auto) on each interface, so it feels like it should answer the question about the protocol in use.
obj-2.4-source-q013.whyWrongHere: show run only shows the static configuration — it doesn't confirm the live, negotiated state of the bundle (whether it actually formed, and with which protocol in practice). show etherchannel gives the real-time operational verification the question is asking about.
obj-2.4-source-q013.memoryAnchor: show run shows what you typed; show etherchannel shows what's actually happening on the wire.
obj-2.4-source-q013.contrast: show run reflects intended configuration; show etherchannel reflects the live, negotiated result — the question asks specifically about verifying, which means live state.

obj-2.4-source-q014.misconceptionReason: Students switch protocol families mid-scenario, answering with PAgP even though the scenario's 'passive' keyword is LACP-specific vocabulary.
obj-2.4-source-q014.whyItSeems: Without a firm anchor on which keywords belong to which protocol, any EtherChannel-related answer can feel plausible, including naming the 'other' protocol.
obj-2.4-source-q014.whyWrongHere: 'Passive' is an LACP mode keyword, not a PAgP one (PAgP uses desirable/auto) — so this scenario is inherently about LACP, not PAgP. And since both sides are passive, no side initiates, so no channel forms at all under LACP.
obj-2.4-source-q014.memoryAnchor: Passive is LACP's word. Two passives = nobody speaks first = no channel — and it's LACP failing, not PAgP running.
obj-2.4-source-q014.contrast: PAgP would need desirable/auto keywords to even be in scope; this scenario's passive/passive keywords keep us in LACP territory, where the result is simply no channel forms.

obj-2.4-source-q014.misconceptionReason: Students assume that because 'passive' is an LACP keyword, some form of LACP channel must still result — missing that passive/passive specifically means neither side initiates.
obj-2.4-source-q014.whyItSeems: It's tempting to think 'well, passive is still an LACP setting, so the answer must involve LACP forming,' without tracing through what passive/passive actually does.
obj-2.4-source-q014.whyWrongHere: LACP passive mode never initiates negotiation on its own — it only responds if the other side starts the conversation. With both sides passive, neither ever sends the first LACP packet, so no PDUs are exchanged and the channel simply never forms.
obj-2.4-source-q014.memoryAnchor: Passive + passive isn't 'LACP, but weaker' — it's no LACP exchange at all, and no channel.
obj-2.4-source-q014.contrast: Active + passive successfully forms an LACP channel because one side initiates; passive + passive forms nothing because neither side ever does.

obj-2.4-source-q014.misconceptionReason: Students confuse LACP's passive mode with the separate 'on' mode, assuming passive somehow forces an unconditional bundle the way on mode does.
obj-2.4-source-q014.whyItSeems: Both 'passive' and 'on' can sound like they mean 'just let it happen without much active effort,' blurring the distinction between a negotiation mode and a no-negotiation mode.
obj-2.4-source-q014.whyWrongHere: Passive is still an LACP negotiation mode — it requires LACP PDUs to be exchanged, which never happens when both sides are passive, so the channel does not form. An unconditional (forced, no-negotiation) port channel only happens with the completely separate on mode on both ends, which was not what was configured here.
obj-2.4-source-q014.memoryAnchor: Passive still needs a negotiation partner to talk to; only 'on' mode skips negotiation and forces the bundle unconditionally.
obj-2.4-source-q014.contrast: on/on forms an unconditional bundle with zero negotiation; passive/passive attempts LACP negotiation but fails because nobody initiates — very different outcomes.

obj-2.4-source-q015.misconceptionReason: Students assume that because a channel does form with on/on, some negotiation protocol must be running underneath it, and default to naming PAgP.
obj-2.4-source-q015.whyItSeems: It's intuitive to assume 'if a bundle exists, some protocol negotiated it,' making it tempting to attribute the result to whichever protocol comes to mind first.
obj-2.4-source-q015.whyWrongHere: On mode specifically bypasses any negotiation protocol — no PAgP hello packets and no LACP PDUs are exchanged. The channel forms unconditionally and statically, based purely on matching configuration, not protocol negotiation.
obj-2.4-source-q015.memoryAnchor: On mode doesn't run PAgP quietly in the background — it runs nothing. The bundle is just forced.
obj-2.4-source-q015.contrast: PAgP would exchange desirable/auto hello packets to negotiate; on/on skips that exchange entirely and simply forces the link up.

obj-2.4-source-q015.misconceptionReason: Students may over-apply the passive/passive failure lesson, mistakenly assuming any pairing involving 'no active negotiation' (like on/on) also fails to form.
obj-2.4-source-q015.whyItSeems: If students just learned that passive/passive fails, it's easy to lump on/on into the same 'nothing happens' bucket without recognizing on mode works completely differently.
obj-2.4-source-q015.whyWrongHere: On mode is not a negotiation mode at all — it doesn't wait for or require any protocol handshake, unlike passive. When both sides match on on, IOS forms the port channel unconditionally and successfully, precisely because there's no negotiation to fail.
obj-2.4-source-q015.memoryAnchor: Passive/passive fails because it waits for a handshake that never comes; on/on succeeds because it skips the handshake altogether.
obj-2.4-source-q015.contrast: Passive/passive is a negotiation mode pairing that can fail to launch; on/on is a non-negotiation mode pairing that always forms a static bundle when matched correctly.

obj-2.4-source-q015.misconceptionReason: Students assume any successfully-formed channel must be running one of the two named protocols (LACP or PAgP), not realizing 'on' mode is a third, protocol-free option.
obj-2.4-source-q015.whyItSeems: LACP and PAgP dominate most EtherChannel teaching, so it's easy to forget that on mode exists as a completely separate, negotiation-free path.
obj-2.4-source-q015.whyWrongHere: LACP requires active/passive mode keywords and actual PDU exchange to negotiate — none of that happens with on mode. Matching on/on forms an unconditional static port channel with no LACP (or PAgP) running at all.
obj-2.4-source-q015.memoryAnchor: On mode isn't 'LACP without the paperwork' — it's a completely different, protocol-free path to the same bundled result.
obj-2.4-source-q015.contrast: LACP forms a channel through active/passive negotiation and ongoing PDU exchange; on/on forms a channel by simply forcing it, with no protocol running in the background.

2.5-c-q1.misconceptionReason: Students blend 'loop' as a generic networking failure concept, assuming STP (a well-known 'loop prevention' technology) must address routing loops too.
2.5-c-q1.whyItSeems: Both routing loops and switching loops are called 'loops' and both are bad — so without distinguishing OSI layers, it's easy to assume one protocol fixes both.
2.5-c-q1.whyWrongHere: Routing loops are a Layer 3 problem, handled by mechanisms like TTL decrementing and routing protocol convergence logic (e.g., split horizon, loop-prevention in EIGRP/OSPF) — STP operates entirely at Layer 2, on switches, and has no visibility into IP routing decisions at all.
2.5-c-q1.memoryAnchor: 'Loop' isn't one thing — Layer 3 loops are a router's problem (TTL, routing protocols); Layer 2 loops are STP's problem.
2.5-c-q1.contrast: Routing loops are prevented by Layer 3 mechanisms like TTL and routing protocol logic; STP specifically blocks redundant Layer 2 switching paths — different layer, different tool.

2.5-c-q1.misconceptionReason: Students lump 'network problems switches/routers solve' together, assuming any switch-adjacent protocol like STP might also police duplicate IP addresses.
2.5-c-q1.whyItSeems: IP conflicts feel like a generic 'bad network thing,' and since STP is also framed as preventing a 'bad network thing' (loops), the two can blur together for someone who hasn't separated the mechanisms.
2.5-c-q1.whyWrongHere: STP operates purely on Layer 2 frame forwarding topology — it has no concept of IP addresses at all. Detecting duplicate IPs is handled by entirely separate mechanisms (like DHCP snooping, Dynamic ARP Inspection, or the OS itself) — not STP.
2.5-c-q1.memoryAnchor: STP never looks at an IP address — it only cares about MAC-level topology and BPDUs.
2.5-c-q1.contrast: IP address conflicts are caught by Layer 3/DHCP-related mechanisms; STP's entire job is preventing Layer 2 frames from looping — it doesn't inspect IP headers at all.

2.5-c-q1.misconceptionReason: Students pick an unrelated network symptom, possibly pattern-matching 'network problem' answer choices without connecting STP's actual mechanism (blocking redundant physical paths) to what it prevents.
2.5-c-q1.whyItSeems: DNS slowness is a real, familiar network complaint, so as a distractor it can seem plausible if a student is unsure and just picks any 'network issue' sounding option.
2.5-c-q1.whyWrongHere: DNS resolution speed depends on the DNS server and application-layer traffic — it's unrelated to Layer 2 topology. STP's actual purpose is preventing broadcast/multicast storms and frame loops that result from physically redundant switch links.
2.5-c-q1.memoryAnchor: STP has nothing to do with name resolution — it's strictly about stopping frames from circling a physically looped topology.
2.5-c-q1.contrast: DNS slowness is an application/Layer 7 concern tied to name servers; STP loop prevention is a Layer 2 concern tied to physical switch topology — completely different layers and causes.

2.5-c-q2.misconceptionReason: Students assume 'highest' wins by default, applying a common 'bigger number wins' intuition without knowing STP specifically favors the lowest value.
2.5-c-q2.whyItSeems: In many contexts (scores, rankings), higher numbers 'win,' so it's an intuitive but backwards assumption for a metric named 'priority.'
2.5-c-q2.whyWrongHere: STP root election explicitly favors the lowest Bridge ID — which combines the numeric priority value (default 32768) with the switch's MAC address. A switch with a lower priority number becomes root, not a higher one.
2.5-c-q2.memoryAnchor: In STP, lower always wins the root race — 'priority' is really a rank where smaller is better.
2.5-c-q2.contrast: Highest priority would suggest 'biggest number wins'; STP's actual rule is the opposite — the switch with the lowest Bridge ID (priority + MAC) becomes root.

2.5-c-q2.misconceptionReason: Students remember that MAC address is a tiebreaker in root election and assume it's the sole deciding factor, and further assume 'highest' wins rather than 'lowest.'
2.5-c-q2.whyItSeems: MAC address genuinely does play a role as the tiebreaker when priorities are equal, so isolating just that piece (and guessing 'highest') feels like a reasonable partial memory.
2.5-c-q2.whyWrongHere: MAC address is only used as a tiebreaker after priority — the full metric is Bridge ID (priority, then MAC), and within that, the lowest value always wins, whether that's the priority portion or the MAC tiebreaker.
2.5-c-q2.memoryAnchor: MAC only matters when priorities tie — and even then, lowest MAC wins, not highest.
2.5-c-q2.contrast: 'Highest MAC' ignores that priority is compared first, and gets the direction backwards — root election is always about the lowest combined Bridge ID.

2.5-c-q2.misconceptionReason: Students assume STP elects a 'best' or 'most capable' switch as root, similar to how some other network protocols might pick a device based on performance characteristics.
2.5-c-q2.whyItSeems: It intuitively makes sense that the 'leader' of a network topology should be the most powerful device, mirroring real-world leadership selection.
2.5-c-q2.whyWrongHere: STP's root election is a purely numeric comparison of Bridge ID (priority + MAC address) — CPU speed, switch model, or performance characteristics play no role whatsoever in the algorithm.
2.5-c-q2.memoryAnchor: STP doesn't care how powerful a switch is — only its Bridge ID number matters.
2.5-c-q2.contrast: Choosing a 'best' device by capability is how some systems elect a leader; STP's root election is a pure numeric comparison of Bridge ID, with no regard for hardware performance.

2.5-c-q3.misconceptionReason: Students confuse 'the best possible priority a switch could be configured to' with 'what a switch ships with by default,' assuming the theoretical minimum is also the factory setting.
2.5-c-q3.whyItSeems: 0 is the lowest (best) value in the priority range, so it can feel like the 'natural' starting point a switch should have.
2.5-c-q3.whyWrongHere: 0 is a valid, and the most preferred, priority value you could manually configure, but it is not the factory default. Cisco switches ship with a default STP priority of 32768.
2.5-c-q3.memoryAnchor: 0 is the best you could set it to; 32768 is what it actually starts at.
2.5-c-q3.contrast: 0 represents the theoretical best-case priority a switch could be configured with; 32768 is the actual out-of-box default before any administrator makes changes.

2.5-c-q3.misconceptionReason: Students recall 4096 as a meaningful STP-related number (the increment used when adjusting priority) and mistake it for the default value itself.
2.5-c-q3.whyItSeems: 4096 genuinely appears in STP contexts — it's the step size Cisco commands use to lower priority (e.g., root primary/secondary macros) — so it's easy to misremember it as 'the' number rather than 'a' number.
2.5-c-q3.whyWrongHere: 4096 is the increment size used when adjusting priority values (valid priorities are multiples of 4096) — it isn't the default value itself. The actual default priority is 32768.
2.5-c-q3.memoryAnchor: 4096 is the step size you move in; 32768 is where every switch starts before you move it.
2.5-c-q3.contrast: 4096 describes how priority values are incremented (0, 4096, 8192, ... up to 61440); 32768 is the specific default value every switch begins at.

2.5-c-q3.misconceptionReason: Students pick the maximum value representable in a 16-bit field, assuming the 'default' must be the largest technically possible number.
2.5-c-q3.whyItSeems: 65535 is the familiar max value of an unsigned 16-bit integer, a number students often encounter in networking contexts (like port ranges), making it feel like a plausible ceiling.
2.5-c-q3.whyWrongHere: STP's valid priority range actually tops out at 61440 (in increments of 4096) — 65535 isn't even a valid configurable STP priority value, let alone the default. The real default is 32768.
2.5-c-q3.memoryAnchor: 65535 is a 16-bit max you might know from elsewhere — STP priority doesn't even go that high; its default is 32768.
2.5-c-q3.contrast: 65535 is a generic 16-bit maximum with no STP-specific meaning; 32768 is the specific, documented default bridge priority within STP's actual 0–61440 valid range.

2.5-c-q4.misconceptionReason: Students confuse the two most commonly discussed STP port roles, mixing up which one faces the root and which one faces away from it.
2.5-c-q4.whyItSeems: Designated port and root port are taught together as 'the two forwarding roles,' so it's easy to swap their directional meaning under exam pressure.
2.5-c-q4.whyWrongHere: A designated port is the best path facing away from the root on a given network segment (there can be many of these). The single port on each non-root switch facing toward the root is specifically called the root port — there's exactly one per non-root switch.
2.5-c-q4.memoryAnchor: Root port points toward the root; designated port points away from it — and every non-root switch has just one root port.
2.5-c-q4.contrast: A switch can have several designated ports (one per outward-facing segment it wins) but only ever one root port (its single best path inward toward the root).

2.5-c-q4.misconceptionReason: Students confuse port state (blocking) with port role (root/designated/alternate), assuming 'blocking' describes the one special port every switch has toward the root.
2.5-c-q4.whyItSeems: Blocking is a well-known STP term, so if a student hasn't distinguished 'role' from 'state,' it can feel like a valid catch-all answer.
2.5-c-q4.whyWrongHere: Blocking is a port state (it stops forwarding to prevent a loop), not the specific role describing a switch's one path toward the root. That specific role — exactly one per non-root switch — is called the root port, and it is always in a forwarding state, not blocking.
2.5-c-q4.memoryAnchor: Blocking describes what a port does (stay quiet); root port describes what a port is for (the path to root) — different categories entirely.
2.5-c-q4.contrast: A blocking port is deliberately not forwarding, to prevent a loop; a root port is actively forwarding, because it's the switch's best (and only) path to the root.

2.5-c-q4.misconceptionReason: Students confuse an interface configuration mode (trunk, carrying multiple VLANs) with an STP-specific port role, treating them as the same kind of category.
2.5-c-q4.whyItSeems: Trunk ports and STP roles are both discussed in switching chapters, so without separating 'how the port is configured' from 'what STP calls it,' the terms can blend together.
2.5-c-q4.whyWrongHere: 'Trunk' describes an interface's VLAN tagging mode (802.1Q) — it says nothing about STP topology roles. STP's specific term for the one port per non-root switch pointing toward the root is the root port; a port can be trunk-configured and still hold any STP role.
2.5-c-q4.memoryAnchor: Trunk is about VLAN tagging; root port is about STP topology — a trunk port can be a root port, but the words aren't interchangeable.
2.5-c-q4.contrast: Trunk mode determines whether 802.1Q tags travel across the link; the root port role determines which single interface is this switch's best path to the STP root — independent classifications.

2.5-c-q5.misconceptionReason: Students think PortFast is a general speed-boosting feature that should be applied wherever fast convergence matters most, including the busiest inter-switch links.
2.5-c-q5.whyItSeems: Trunk links between switches are often the most performance-critical, so it can feel logical to want the 'fast' feature applied there first.
2.5-c-q5.whyWrongHere: PortFast skips the STP listening/learning delay because it assumes the port connects to a single end host that can't create a loop. A switch-to-switch trunk can absolutely be part of a loop, so enabling PortFast there risks a temporary loop if BPDUs are missed during a topology change — PortFast belongs only on access ports facing end devices.
2.5-c-q5.memoryAnchor: PortFast assumes 'nothing but one host is here' — a trunk to another switch breaks that assumption immediately.
2.5-c-q5.contrast: Trunk links interconnect switches and must go through STP's normal listening/learning states to safely detect loops; access ports to end hosts can safely skip those states because a PC or phone can't form a loop.

2.5-c-q5.misconceptionReason: Students assume any 'important' or 'always up' link — like a router uplink — is a good candidate for PortFast's faster transition.
2.5-c-q5.whyItSeems: Router uplinks are critical, always-on connections, so it might seem beneficial to make them come up as fast as possible, similar to PortFast's purpose for end devices.
2.5-c-q5.whyWrongHere: PortFast's use case is specifically single-host access ports where a genuine STP loop is impossible — Cisco's guidance targets ports connecting to PCs, phones, and servers, not router uplinks (which are typically part of a more complex, potentially loop-capable topology).
2.5-c-q5.memoryAnchor: PortFast targets the edge (PCs, phones, servers), not uplinks to other network devices.
2.5-c-q5.contrast: A router uplink is a network-to-network connection that STP still needs to evaluate through its normal states; an access port to an end host is the safe, intended target for PortFast's shortcut.

2.5-c-q5.misconceptionReason: Students treat PortFast as a universal performance upgrade that should be turned on everywhere for maximum speed, without considering the loop-safety tradeoff it makes.
2.5-c-q5.whyItSeems: 'Faster is always better' is an intuitive but incomplete way to think about a feature that trades off loop-detection safety for speed.
2.5-c-q5.whyWrongHere: Applying PortFast everywhere — including switch-to-switch links — removes STP's safety checks on ports that could actually participate in a loop, creating real risk of a temporary broadcast storm. PortFast is intended only for access ports where end devices connect, not universally.
2.5-c-q5.memoryAnchor: PortFast trades loop-safety for speed — that trade is only safe on ports where a loop genuinely can't form.
2.5-c-q5.contrast: Applying PortFast to every port ignores where loops can actually occur; restricting it to end-device access ports keeps the safety net intact everywhere a loop is actually possible.

2.5-c-q6.misconceptionReason: Students assume receiving a BPDU on a PortFast port must trigger a root-election-style response, since BPDUs are strongly associated with electing a root bridge.
2.5-c-q6.whyItSeems: BPDUs are the packets used in root election, so it seems plausible that receiving one would somehow feed into that same election process on this port.
2.5-c-q6.whyWrongHere: BPDU Guard's entire purpose is to treat any BPDU on a PortFast (end-host) port as evidence something is wrong — a rogue switch has been plugged in where only a host was expected. Instead of processing it for root election, BPDU Guard immediately err-disables (shuts down) the port.
2.5-c-q6.memoryAnchor: On a PortFast+BPDU Guard port, seeing a BPDU isn't an invitation to negotiate — it's an alarm that shuts the port down.
2.5-c-q6.contrast: Normal STP ports would process a BPDU as part of root election; a PortFast+BPDU Guard port treats that same BPDU as a violation and disables itself instead.

2.5-c-q6.misconceptionReason: Students assume switches forward everything they receive by default, applying general Layer 2 frame-forwarding logic to what is actually a protective control-plane feature.
2.5-c-q6.whyItSeems: Switches do forward most frames they don't recognize as 'theirs,' so forwarding a BPDU can feel like the default, unremarkable behavior.
2.5-c-q6.whyWrongHere: BPDU Guard is a specific safeguard designed to catch and stop unexpected BPDUs on access ports — it doesn't pass them along into the STP domain. Instead, receiving any BPDU on a BPDU Guard-protected port immediately err-disables that port.
2.5-c-q6.memoryAnchor: BPDU Guard doesn't relay the BPDU anywhere — it shuts the door on the port that received it.
2.5-c-q6.contrast: A trunk port between switches normally participates fully in BPDU exchange; a BPDU Guard-protected access port is specifically configured to never tolerate or pass along a BPDU at all — it shuts down instead.

2.5-c-q6.misconceptionReason: Students assume PortFast means 'STP is completely turned off' on that port, so nothing happens even if a BPDU shows up.
2.5-c-q6.whyItSeems: PortFast does skip STP's listening/learning delay, so it's easy to over-extend that idea into 'STP is fully ignored' on that port.
2.5-c-q6.whyWrongHere: PortFast only skips the initial forwarding delay — it doesn't disable STP monitoring altogether, especially when paired with BPDU Guard. BPDU Guard actively watches for any BPDU on that port and, if one arrives, immediately err-disables the interface — this is a real, active response, not a no-op.
2.5-c-q6.memoryAnchor: PortFast skips the wait; BPDU Guard still watches — receiving a BPDU is never a non-event on a protected port.
2.5-c-q6.contrast: PortFast alone (without BPDU Guard) might tolerate an occasional BPDU without shutting the port down; PortFast combined with BPDU Guard treats that same BPDU as an immediate trigger to err-disable the port.

2.5-c-q7.misconceptionReason: Students recall 802.1D as 'the' STP standard from foundational lessons and assume it's still what Cisco switches run by default today.
2.5-c-q7.whyItSeems: 802.1D is the original, most commonly cited STP specification in intro material, so it's the natural first answer when asked about 'the' default.
