2.5-c-q7.whyWrongHere: 802.1D is the classic, original STP standard, but modern Cisco switches don't default to running it in its original slow-converging form — they default to Rapid PVST+, which behaves like 802.1w (RSTP) on a per-VLAN basis.
2.5-c-q7.memoryAnchor: 802.1D is the ancestor everyone learns first; Rapid PVST+ is what's actually running by default today.
2.5-c-q7.contrast: 802.1D is the historical baseline standard with 30-50 second convergence; Rapid PVST+ is Cisco's current default, converging far faster on a per-VLAN basis.

2.5-c-q7.misconceptionReason: Students remember MST as a more 'advanced' or 'modern-sounding' spanning-tree mode and assume newer must mean default.
2.5-c-q7.whyItSeems: MST is often taught as the most scalable, sophisticated STP variant, so it can seem like the logical 'upgrade path' a vendor would default to.
2.5-c-q7.whyWrongHere: MST (802.1s) maps multiple VLANs to a smaller number of spanning-tree instances — it's powerful for large networks but requires explicit configuration; it is not what Catalyst switches run out of the box. The actual factory default is Rapid PVST+.
2.5-c-q7.memoryAnchor: MST is a deliberate, configured choice for large networks — not the out-of-box default, which is Rapid PVST+.
2.5-c-q7.contrast: MST requires explicit configuration to group VLANs into instances; Rapid PVST+ runs automatically per-VLAN with zero extra configuration, which is why it's the actual factory default.

2.5-c-q7.misconceptionReason: Students recall 'PVST' as a real per-VLAN STP mode but drop the 'Rapid' qualifier, assuming the older, non-rapid version is still the default.
2.5-c-q7.whyItSeems: PVST is genuinely a real, named mode, and it's easy to reach for the simpler name without noticing the missing 'Rapid' prefix changes which protocol version is actually running.
2.5-c-q7.whyWrongHere: Classic PVST runs original 802.1D-style STP per VLAN, with slower convergence. Current Cisco IOS defaults to the faster variant — Rapid PVST+, which uses 802.1w-style rapid convergence per VLAN, not the older non-rapid PVST.
2.5-c-q7.memoryAnchor: Don't drop the word 'Rapid' — PVST and Rapid PVST+ converge at very different speeds, and only Rapid PVST+ is the default.
2.5-c-q7.contrast: Classic PVST converges at 802.1D speed (30-50 seconds) per VLAN; Rapid PVST+ converges at 802.1w speed (seconds) per VLAN — and only the rapid version is Cisco's default.

2.5-c-q8.misconceptionReason: Students conflate 'making STP behave the way I want on this switch' broadly, mistakenly assuming the PortFast command influences root bridge selection.
2.5-c-q8.whyItSeems: Both commands live under the same 'spanning-tree' command family, so it's easy to assume any spanning-tree keyword could plausibly affect who becomes root.
2.5-c-q8.whyWrongHere: spanning-tree portfast only affects how quickly an access port transitions to forwarding — it has zero effect on bridge priority or root election. Becoming root requires lowering this switch's priority specifically, which is exactly what spanning-tree vlan 1 root primary does.
2.5-c-q8.memoryAnchor: PortFast changes port transition speed; root primary changes root election — same command family, completely different jobs.
2.5-c-q8.contrast: spanning-tree portfast speeds up one access port's path to forwarding; spanning-tree vlan 1 root primary lowers this switch's overall priority so it wins the root election for VLAN 1.

2.5-c-q8.misconceptionReason: Students again default to a familiar spanning-tree-related command, assuming any protective STP feature might also influence which switch becomes root.
2.5-c-q8.whyItSeems: BPDU Guard is a commonly taught STP feature, and if a student hasn't clearly separated 'protection' features from 'root election' features, it can seem like a plausible catch-all answer.
2.5-c-q8.whyWrongHere: spanning-tree bpduguard enable protects access ports by shutting them down if they unexpectedly receive a BPDU — it has nothing to do with bridge priority or becoming root. To become root for VLAN 1, you need spanning-tree vlan 1 root primary, which specifically lowers this switch's priority.
2.5-c-q8.memoryAnchor: BPDU Guard protects edge ports from rogue switches; it doesn't touch this switch's own priority or root status.
2.5-c-q8.contrast: spanning-tree bpduguard enable is a defensive feature for access ports; spanning-tree vlan 1 root primary is an offensive command that actively lowers priority to win the root election.

2.5-c-q8.misconceptionReason: Students confuse interface-level VLAN configuration (trunking) with switch-wide STP priority configuration, assuming trunk mode somehow relates to becoming root.
2.5-c-q8.whyItSeems: Trunk links do carry STP BPDUs across VLANs, so it might seem like configuring trunking is somehow tied to influencing STP outcomes like root election.
2.5-c-q8.whyWrongHere: switchport mode trunk simply configures an interface to carry multiple VLANs' traffic (802.1Q tagging) — it has no effect on the switch's STP bridge priority. Becoming root for VLAN 1 requires the dedicated command spanning-tree vlan 1 root primary, which lowers priority specifically.
2.5-c-q8.memoryAnchor: Trunk mode decides what VLANs cross a link; root primary decides which switch wins the root election — unrelated settings.
2.5-c-q8.contrast: switchport mode trunk is an interface-level VLAN tagging configuration; spanning-tree vlan 1 root primary is a switch-wide STP priority configuration — one doesn't substitute for the other.

obj-2.5-source-q001.misconceptionReason: Students recognize 802.1X as a real, well-known IEEE 802.1-series standard and guess it applies here without checking that it actually governs port-based authentication, not spanning tree.
obj-2.5-source-q001.whyItSeems: The shared '802.1' prefix makes it feel related to the same family of switching standards being discussed, even though the specific function is completely different.
obj-2.5-source-q001.whyWrongHere: 802.1X defines port-based network access control (authentication before traffic is allowed) — it has no relationship to loop prevention. The original spanning-tree standard is 802.1D.
obj-2.5-source-q001.memoryAnchor: 802.1X gates who gets on the network; 802.1D stops loops once they're on — different letters, different jobs.
obj-2.5-source-q001.contrast: 802.1X controls whether a device is authenticated onto a port; 802.1D controls how switches avoid Layer 2 loops — sharing the '802.1' prefix doesn't mean sharing a function.

obj-2.5-source-q001.misconceptionReason: Students confuse classic STP with its rapid successor, mixing up which standard number belongs to the original protocol versus the newer, faster-converging one.
obj-2.5-source-q001.whyItSeems: 802.1w and 802.1D are taught together as 'STP and its upgrade,' so their numbers can blur together without a clear anchor for which is which.
obj-2.5-source-q001.whyWrongHere: 802.1w specifically designates Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (RSTP), the faster-converging successor. The original, classic Spanning Tree Protocol standard is 802.1D.
obj-2.5-source-q001.memoryAnchor: 802.1D = the original (slow). 802.1w = the rapid upgrade. Don't hand the classic name to the rapid number.
obj-2.5-source-q001.contrast: 802.1D converges in roughly 30-50 seconds using the original STP algorithm; 802.1w (RSTP) converges much faster with an improved algorithm — this question asks specifically about classic STP, which is 802.1D.

obj-2.5-source-q001.misconceptionReason: Students mix up the Multiple Spanning Tree standard with classic STP, since both are part of the same family of spanning-tree-related IEEE numbers.
obj-2.5-source-q001.whyItSeems: 802.1s is a legitimate spanning-tree-related standard, so without a clear distinction of 'which one is which,' it's a plausible-sounding guess for 'the' STP standard.
obj-2.5-source-q001.whyWrongHere: 802.1s specifically defines Multiple Spanning Tree (MST), which maps many VLANs onto a smaller number of spanning-tree instances — a more advanced, later standard. The original, classic Spanning Tree Protocol is 802.1D.
obj-2.5-source-q001.memoryAnchor: 802.1s = Multiple instances (MST). 802.1D = the original, single-instance STP being asked about here.
obj-2.5-source-q001.contrast: 802.1s (MST) groups VLANs into a handful of spanning-tree instances for scalability; 802.1D is the original, per-bridge classic STP standard this question is asking about.

obj-2.5-source-q002.misconceptionReason: Students imagine STP working like a centralized controller model — one switch computing the topology for everyone else — rather than understanding it as a distributed algorithm.
obj-2.5-source-q002.whyItSeems: Having one elected 'root' switch can make it seem like that switch is doing all the calculating for the whole network, similar to a central controller.
obj-2.5-source-q002.whyWrongHere: While STP does elect a single root bridge as a topology reference point, the actual STP process runs independently on every switch — each one processes incoming BPDUs and builds its own local view of the topology database; there is no single switch computing everything for the network.
obj-2.5-source-q002.memoryAnchor: The root bridge is a reference point, not a central brain — every switch still runs STP itself.
obj-2.5-source-q002.contrast: A central-controller model would have one device compute results for everyone; STP has every switch independently run the same distributed algorithm, each building its own topology view from shared BPDUs.

obj-2.5-source-q002.misconceptionReason: Students associate 'loop prevention' broadly with routing protocol mechanisms (like split horizon or hold-down timers), forgetting that STP is a completely separate, Layer 2-only mechanism.
obj-2.5-source-q002.whyItSeems: Routing protocols do have their own loop-prevention logic, so it can seem plausible that STP might 'borrow' or use similar routing-protocol techniques.
obj-2.5-source-q002.whyWrongHere: STP is entirely a Layer 2 mechanism — it uses its own dedicated frames (BPDUs), not routing protocol messages, to build a topology database and check for loops. Routing protocols operate independently at Layer 3 and have no role in STP's loop detection.
obj-2.5-source-q002.memoryAnchor: STP speaks its own language (BPDUs) — it never borrows a routing protocol's mechanisms.
obj-2.5-source-q002.contrast: Routing protocols prevent Layer 3 loops using their own protocol-specific rules (metrics, split horizon, etc.); STP prevents Layer 2 loops using its own protocol-specific BPDUs — the two never intermix.

obj-2.5-source-q002.misconceptionReason: Students conflate STP's loop-prevention logic with the switch's normal frame-forwarding mechanism (the MAC/CAM table), assuming the same table used for forwarding also detects loops.
obj-2.5-source-q002.whyItSeems: Both STP and MAC learning are core switch behaviors happening 'under the hood,' so it's easy to merge them into one imagined unified mechanism.
obj-2.5-source-q002.whyWrongHere: The MAC address table is used purely for frame-forwarding decisions (which port to send a frame out) — it plays no role in loop detection. STP builds a completely separate topology database from BPDU exchanges specifically to identify and prevent loops.
obj-2.5-source-q002.memoryAnchor: MAC table = 'where do I send this frame.' STP topology database = 'is there a loop in my topology.' Two separate jobs.
obj-2.5-source-q002.contrast: The MAC table tracks which port leads to which MAC address for forwarding; STP's topology database tracks bridge/port relationships from BPDUs specifically to detect and block loops — different data, different purposes.

obj-2.5-source-q003.misconceptionReason: Students assume STP inspects regular user data traffic to detect duplicate paths, mixing up the control plane (BPDUs) with the data plane (user frames).
obj-2.5-source-q003.whyItSeems: A loop is ultimately experienced as ordinary traffic circulating endlessly, so it can seem intuitive that STP would watch that same traffic to detect the problem.
obj-2.5-source-q003.whyWrongHere: STP doesn't inspect ordinary data frames at all — its loop detection relies entirely on a dedicated control-plane message type, BPDUs, sent between switches. Seeing BPDUs arrive from multiple directions (implying multiple paths) is what signals a potential loop, not the behavior of user traffic.
obj-2.5-source-q003.memoryAnchor: STP watches its own control messages (BPDUs), not the user traffic riding on top of the network.
obj-2.5-source-q003.contrast: Ordinary data frames are what would actually loop and flood if STP failed; BPDUs are the separate, dedicated messages STP uses to detect that risk before it happens.

obj-2.5-source-q003.misconceptionReason: Students confuse two different Cisco/IEEE Layer 2 protocols — CDP (neighbor discovery) and STP (loop prevention) — assuming they might share the same monitoring mechanism.
obj-2.5-source-q003.whyItSeems: Both CDP and STP frames travel between adjacent switches at Layer 2, so without separating their purposes, it's easy to assume one protocol's frames serve the other's function.
obj-2.5-source-q003.whyWrongHere: CDP frames exist purely to advertise neighbor information (device type, capabilities, addresses) — they have nothing to do with loop detection. STP's loop detection relies specifically on its own dedicated BPDU frames, not CDP.
obj-2.5-source-q003.memoryAnchor: CDP tells you who your neighbor is; BPDUs tell STP whether there's a loop — completely different message types, completely different jobs.
obj-2.5-source-q003.contrast: CDP frames advertise device identity and capabilities between neighbors; BPDUs carry the topology and root-bridge information STP actually needs to detect and prevent loops.

obj-2.5-source-q003.misconceptionReason: Students imagine STP tracking VLAN membership across access ports as its loop-detection mechanism, confusing VLAN scope with the actual BPDU-based control plane.
obj-2.5-source-q003.whyItSeems: Loops are often discussed in the context of a specific VLAN's broadcast domain, so it can feel plausible that STP 'watches VLAN membership' rather than a specific message type.
obj-2.5-source-q003.whyWrongHere: STP's detection mechanism isn't about which VLAN an access port belongs to — it's about BPDU exchange between switches (or per-VLAN instances in Rapid PVST+). Access port VLAN assignment is a completely separate configuration concept from how STP actually senses a loop.
obj-2.5-source-q003.memoryAnchor: VLAN membership defines broadcast domains; BPDU exchange is what STP actually watches to catch a loop.
obj-2.5-source-q003.contrast: Access port VLAN assignment determines which broadcast domain a port belongs to; STP's BPDU monitoring determines whether that domain (or the switch topology generally) contains a redundant, loop-forming path.

obj-2.5-source-q004.misconceptionReason: Students again pull in the familiar 802.1X standard simply because it shares the '802.1' family prefix, without recognizing it governs authentication, not spanning tree.
obj-2.5-source-q004.whyItSeems: The shared numbering prefix creates a false sense of relatedness among all 802.1-series standards.
obj-2.5-source-q004.whyWrongHere: 802.1X is entirely about port-based network access control (authentication) — it has no relationship to spanning-tree convergence behavior. The IEEE standard for Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol is 802.1w.
obj-2.5-source-q004.memoryAnchor: 802.1X authenticates; 802.1w converges spanning tree quickly — unrelated functions sharing only a numbering family.
obj-2.5-source-q004.contrast: 802.1X decides whether a device is allowed onto a port at all; 802.1w decides how fast a switched topology recovers from a link change — entirely separate concerns.

obj-2.5-source-q004.misconceptionReason: Students mix up the classic and rapid STP standards, assuming the original 802.1D designation also covers the 'rapid' improved version.
obj-2.5-source-q004.whyItSeems: 802.1D and 802.1w are directly related (RSTP evolved from STP), so it's easy to misassign the wrong number to the 'rapid' variant if the two aren't clearly separated in memory.
obj-2.5-source-q004.whyWrongHere: 802.1D is specifically the original, classic Spanning Tree Protocol standard, with its slower (30-50 second) convergence behavior. The faster-converging Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol has its own distinct designation: 802.1w.
obj-2.5-source-q004.memoryAnchor: 802.1D is the original tortoise; 802.1w is the rapid hare — different numbers for different convergence speeds.
obj-2.5-source-q004.contrast: 802.1D describes the original STP algorithm and its slower convergence; 802.1w describes the specific rapid-reconvergence improvements that define RSTP.

obj-2.5-source-q004.misconceptionReason: Students confuse RSTP with MST, since both are 'improvements on classic STP' conceptually, without separating rapid convergence (802.1w) from multi-instance VLAN mapping (802.1s).
obj-2.5-source-q004.whyItSeems: Both 802.1w and 802.1s are more 'modern' spanning-tree-related standards discussed in the same lesson, so their numbers can be swapped without careful attention.
obj-2.5-source-q004.whyWrongHere: 802.1s specifically defines Multiple Spanning Tree (MST) — grouping many VLANs into fewer spanning-tree instances for scalability. It's a separate concern from convergence speed. The standard for Rapid Spanning Tree specifically is 802.1w.
obj-2.5-source-q004.memoryAnchor: 802.1s = Multiple instances (MST, about scale). 802.1w = Rapid (RSTP, about speed). Different problems, different numbers.
obj-2.5-source-q004.contrast: 802.1s solves the problem of running fewer STP instances across many VLANs; 802.1w solves the problem of converging faster after a topology change — this question asks specifically about the rapid-convergence standard, which is 802.1w.

obj-2.5-source-q005.misconceptionReason: Students assume 'cost' in a networking context must reflect a real-time performance metric like delay or latency, since that's a common meaning of 'cost' in other routing contexts.
obj-2.5-source-q005.whyItSeems: Some routing metrics (like OSPF's use of bandwidth-derived cost, or EIGRP's composite metric including delay) do factor in delay-like values, so it's plausible to assume STP's cost works similarly.
obj-2.5-source-q005.whyWrongHere: STP's link cost isn't a measured, real-time latency value — it's a fixed numeric value derived directly from the link's configured or negotiated speed (higher bandwidth links get a lower cost value). It doesn't change based on actual frame transit delay.
obj-2.5-source-q005.memoryAnchor: STP cost is about bandwidth, not delay — a value looked up from link speed, not measured in real time.
obj-2.5-source-q005.contrast: Latency would be a dynamic, measured value reflecting actual transit time; STP link cost is a static value assigned based on the link's speed, following a standard table (e.g., 100 Mb/s vs. 1 Gb/s).

obj-2.5-source-q005.misconceptionReason: Students confuse the definition of a single link's cost with the definition of overall path cost, which is the sum of link costs along the entire route to the root.
obj-2.5-source-q005.whyItSeems: Both terms ('link cost' and 'path cost') are closely related and used together constantly in STP discussions, making it easy to define one in terms of the other's actual meaning.
obj-2.5-source-q005.whyWrongHere: Summing the cost of every port along the route to the root describes path cost, a separate (though related) concept — it's the total, not the definition of an individual link's cost. Link cost itself is simply the per-port numeric value tied to that link's speed.
obj-2.5-source-q005.memoryAnchor: Link cost is one port's number; path cost is those numbers added up along the whole route to root.
obj-2.5-source-q005.contrast: Path cost is the STP metric compared during root port selection, built by adding up individual link costs; link cost itself is just the per-link value (based on speed) that feeds into that sum.

obj-2.5-source-q005.misconceptionReason: Students take the everyday meaning of 'cost' (money) too literally, rather than recognizing it as networking jargon for a technical metric.
obj-2.5-source-q005.whyItSeems: 'Cost' is a common financial term in everyday language, so without networking context, it's a reasonable literal misreading.
obj-2.5-source-q005.whyWrongHere: In STP, 'cost' is purely a technical metric with no financial meaning whatsoever — it's a numeric value assigned based on link speed, used to compare paths during the STP algorithm, not an actual dollar figure or expense.
obj-2.5-source-q005.memoryAnchor: STP cost has nothing to do with money — it's a technical number tied to bandwidth.
obj-2.5-source-q005.contrast: A monetary cost would reflect actual dollars spent on equipment or circuits; STP link cost is a purely technical value derived from link speed, used only within the spanning-tree algorithm's math.
